Hi everyone,

I am a professor at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou). My students and I are very excited about Lean and CSLib. We believe it is important to enhance this knowledge base and provide infrastructure for using formalized results in real-world verification projects. We would be very interested in contributing to CSLib @Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai @Chris Henson

Our research areas include quantum computing, quantum algorithms, and quantum information theory. We have been developing Lean-QuantumAlg, a Lean 4 library of formally verified quantum algorithms covering standard algorithms such as Deutsch–Jozsa, Bernstein–Vazirani, QFT, QSP, order finding, and reusable primitives, with a pure-state and unitary-gate core. For more information about the included formalized results, please see our website.

The CSLib whitepaper lists quantum computation as an in-scope model, so we would love to explore contributing this work as a quantum algorithms area. Following the CONTRIBUTING guidelines, I wanted to check here before beginning any migration work:

  • Scope — Would a quantum algorithms area be welcome at this stage?
  • Placement — If so, should it be placed under Cslib/QuantumComputing/, or under Cslib/Algorithms/Quantum/?
  • Process — Are there any preferences regarding PR size and the contents of the first PR, or anything else we should know before getting started?

Github repo: https://github.com/QudeLeap/Lean-QuantumAlg
Documentation: https://qudeleap.github.io/Lean-QuantumAlg

Thank you very much for your time. We look forward to hearing from you.

Thank you for the message. The repo looks quite good quality. Quantum algorithms are very welcome. The starting point should be just to PR basic definitions of your repo into cslib. I am happy to discuss more if you are interested.

I wish to point out that there are multiple groups of physicists and computer scientists who are independently working on formalising quantum algorithms (including mine, presented at the STOC workshop on "can AI do theory" two days ago). Ideally CSLib should receive multiple proposals and choose the most general among them.
I also have a library, and a few other groups too. It would be good to coordinate between the groups working on this.
@Bas Spitters I'll start a topic in #computer science for this
Here's a link to the thread : #computer science > Writing quantum algorithms in lean @ 💬
I have grown confused by the proliferation of people doing quantum w/ Lean. I made this list: https://ohaithe.re/quantum_lean_repos

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Ideally CSLib should receive multiple proposals and choose the most general among them.

This is certainly how we should proceed, especially given the variety of formulations that have been pointed out. (Though I fear there is a bit of an xkcd 927 situation already)

I took a look at this repository. It needs a lot of work and design improvements before it is ready for CSLib PRs. Just two examples: I am not sure why it needs a layer of abbreviation for TimeM. I am also not sure where this file defines deutsch Jozsa. As a computer scientist writing an algorithm I would expect to see the three-four line algorithm in one place

https://github.com/QudeLeap/Lean-QuantumAlg/blob/main/QuantumAlg/Algorithms/DeutschJozsa.lean

Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai said:

The starting point should be just to PR basic definitions of your repo into cslib.

Thank you! We've filed an issue and a corresponding pull request following your suggestion.

Chris Henson said:

Though I fear there is a bit of an xkcd 927 situation already

We share the same concern. This PR contains only foundational types for pure-state unitary quantum computing (registers, states, and gates), without imposing any framework on top. This provides a small starting point.
All of this already exists in multiple libraries. Ideally you want to use physlib’s definitions for the basics.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

All of this already exists in multiple libraries. Ideally you want to use physlib’s definitions for the basics.

I think we should definitely try this, though it requires some thought towards dependencies and library scopes. Let me think about this a bit and maybe I'll post a thread in the Physlib channel to get their thoughts.

@Shreyas Srinivas Thank you for these comments.

  • A layer of abbreviation is just used for cleaness, and will be removed once related contents are purposed to be merged in CSLib.
  • We have improved the algorithm presentation (see the updated documentaiton). Any comments are sincerely welcome :smiley:

For PhysLib, our impression is not to include them. One major reason is that QuantumInfo in Physlib is from the perspective of quantum operators (density operators, quantum channel, CPTP, channel capacity, etc.). These things are not suitable for quantum algorithms, at least for existing quantum algorithms.
I disagree with your claim about the suitability of quantum operators, having already observed multiple people do so, but let’s save that discussion for another topic.
In fact you might want to post your case for the unsuitability of operators here. Multiple physicists are also working on this : #computer science > Writing quantum algorithms in lean

Chris Henson said:

Shreyas Srinivas said:

All of this already exists in multiple libraries. Ideally you want to use physlib’s definitions for the basics.

I think we should definitely try this, though it requires some thought towards dependencies and library scopes. Let me think about this a bit and maybe I'll post a thread in the Physlib channel to get their thoughts.

One obstacle that might be encountered is physlib skips updates to RC toolchains. I have had suboptimal experiences with the docs CI when mixing cslib and physlib dependencies as a result.

Xin Wang (HKUST-GZ) said:

For PhysLib, our impression is not to include them. One major reason is that QuantumInfo in Physlib is from the perspective of quantum operators (density operators, quantum channel, CPTP, channel capacity, etc.). These things are not suitable for quantum algorithms, at least for existing quantum algorithms.

I'm quite confused what you mean! I regularly think of quantum algorithms as using density operators. There are handful that can be accomplished without intermediate measurements or POVMs, but Physlib also has pure states, ways to link them to density operators, and basic instances of unitary gates and so on.

And if there's some formalism that you need that is really incompatible with density operators, it would be a welcome PR to Physlib. :)

Actually, for that matter, much of this content is probably generally welcome anyway! :smiley:

Alex Meiburg said in #Physlib > List of quantum/lean repos:

Update: In the two days since I posted this, two more repositories of interest have popped up:

  • https://github.com/Paul-Lez/QLean, from Paul Lezeau
  • https://github.com/urikol/QuantumOptimization/tree/main, from Dirk Englund's group (for the very cool paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29687)

Bas Spitters said:

I also have a library, and a few other groups too. It would be good to coordinate between the groups working on this.

I think that would be nice! Happy to collaborate with other groups/merge stuff together/whatever other people think is best:)
